# A BRIEF SUMMARY
## Of the
# RELIGION
## Of the
# TURKS.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' inside a square border, embellished with ornate floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>

*The Turks believe in one single God, in one single Person, Creator of Heaven and of Earth; Rewarder of the good, and Punisher of the evil; who has created Paradise to reward the pious: and Hell for the ultimate punishment of crimes. They believe that Mahomet <note>The historical Dutch spelling for Muhammad</note> is a very great Prophet, and that God has sent him into the World to teach mankind the way of salvation. They call themselves Muselmannen <note>Muslims</note>, that is, those who have surrendered themselves to God's will, or the Blessed.*

*They believe in the ten commandments of Moses, and are obliged to keep them. They observe Friday, just as the Christians do Sunday: On this day they gather in the Churches <note>referring here to Mosques</note> at noon to perform their prayers.*

*They are obliged to perform their prayers five times a day, namely in the morning, at noon*

## Short Summary.

They fast during the Month or Moon, which they call Ramazan <note>Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar</note>. In this Month they neither eat nor drink anything during the day, until the Sun has set; but at night they eat and drink according to their desire and pleasure Meat and Fish, except for Pork-meat, and Wine; which is always forbidden to them. After this Fast they have the festival of the great Bairan <note>Eid al-Fitr, the "Festival of Breaking the Fast"</note>, just as the Christians have the festival of Easter after Lent. They are great builders of Churches <note>Mosques</note> and Hospitals, and must on the first day of the year give a tenth of what they have earned in the previous year to the poor.

They believe that, when they have washed their bodies well, and have spoken a prayer suited for that purpose, their soul is also free from all kinds of sins and stains; which is the reason that they wash and bathe themselves often, especially before they perform their prayers.

They have no other Sacrament than Circumcision. They have their Children circumcised at the age of seven or eight years, and when they can speak these words: *La ilha illa allha Mehemet rasoul allha*: that is, there is no more than one God, and Mahomet is his Prophet and Apostle; which is their Confession of faith <note>The Shahada, the Islamic declaration of belief</note>. There is, however, no mention made of Circumcision in the entire Alkoran <note>The Quran</note>: but they

### Brief Summary.

<margin>R 40</margin>They say that they maintain such practices following the example of Abraham, whose Law was commended to them by Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>. They believe that the Quran <note>original: "Alkoran"</note> was brought to him at various times by the Angel Gabriel, in the Cities of Mecca and Medina, because the Jews and Christians had altered the Holy Scriptures and God's Law.

They are permitted to have four married wives at the same time, and as many enslaved daughters and women as they are able to provide for.

They may leave their wives whenever it seems good to them, provided they pay them that which they promised by marriage-contract, and may marry again at their pleasure. However, the women are required to wait until it is certain that they are not pregnant before they marry again; and the men are required to keep the children and take care of them. The children they have by their enslaved women are treated exactly the same as those they have by their married wives, and all are considered legitimate.

They have churches <note>The author uses "Kerken" to refer to mosques</note>, assemblies, and hospitals which have good incomes, and also cloisters of clergy <note>likely referring to Sufi dervishes or religious orders</note> who serve as a good example to others. They obey their superiors without contradiction, and dance to the sound of flutes and other instruments <note>original: "gereetschap"</note> when they perform their prayers.

It also describes religious infrastructure and the ritual practices of certain orders, likely dervishes.</summary>

## Short Summary.

They have yet another kind of Clergy <note>original: "Geestelijken"; here referring to dervishes or wandering ascetics</note> who roam through the world, who are dressed like the Fools of this Land. They often go naked and cut into their flesh in various places. They are held to be holy people and live on alms, which are never refused to them. Both these kinds of religious orders call themselves Dervishes <note>original: "Dervis"</note>: one recognizes them by their clothes, and they may depart [from their order] and marry as it seems good to them.

They do not believe that Jesus Christ is God, nor God's Son, and they also do not believe in the Holy Trinity. They say that Jesus Christ is a great Prophet, born of the Virgin Mary—a Virgin before and after the birth: that he was conceived without a Father through Divine inspiration, or through a Divine breath; just as Adam was created without a Mother: that he was not crucified, but that God has raised him up to Heaven, and that he shall come back to Earth before the end of the World to confirm Muhammad's Law <note>original: "Mahomets Wet"; referring to the teachings of Islam</note>. They also assert that the Jews, intending to crucify Jesus Christ, crucified a man among them who resembled him.

They pray to God for the Deceased: they call upon their Saints, of whom they have a long account. They do not, however, believe in Purgatory <note>original: "Vagevuur"</note>; and many of them consider that the souls and bodies remain together in the grave until the Day of Judgment.

<keywords>Dervishes, asceticism, Christology in Islam, Virgin Mary, crucifixion, Day of Judgment, intercession for the dead</keywords>

### Short Summary.

They hold Mecca and Medina, two cities of Arabia, in great reverence, because Muhammad was born in Mecca and buried in Medina. They make great pilgrimages to those places and consider that land to be holy. They also show great reverence to the city of Jerusalem, because it was the birthplace and dwelling of many Prophets.

They do not have the use of bells; but their priests <note>The author refers to the Muezzin, who calls the faithful to prayer</note> climb at the hour of their prayers to the highest point of a tower <note>minaret</note>, which is located in one of the corners of the church <note>mosque</note>, and call the people to prayer with a loud voice, and sing prayers that have been prepared for that purpose.

### VI. Chapter of the Forecourt of Hell, containing one hundred and six lines, written at Mecca.

Dear Reader, Mahomet has called this chapter the Chapter of Aaraf <note>original: "Aaraf" - referring to Al-A'raf, the "Heights" or partition between heaven and hell in Islamic theology</note>, which is a place between Paradise and Hell, where people suffer no pain. See the Mokari, the Bedaoi, and Kitabel tenoir <note>These refer to classical Islamic commentaries (Tafsir) and scholars, likely Al-Bukhari, Al-Baydawi, and Kitab al-Tanwir.</note>.

In the name of the gracious and merciful God. I am the wisest and truest God. This book is sent to you, to preach to the true believers; Do not doubt that which it contains within itself. Say to them: Believe in that which is sent on behalf of your Lord; worship no other God but him. There are few people among you who reflect upon it. How many cities have we destroyed? ### IX. *Chapter of Jonah, containing one hundred and nine verses, written at Mecca.*

In the name of the kind and merciful God. I am the merciful God. The commandments contained in this book proceed from the Almighty. Shall the people be wondered <note>surprised or astonished</note> that we have inspired a man to proclaim the pains of hell to the wicked, and to announce to the true believers that they shall find the truth of that which their Lord has promised them? The wicked say that there is nothing here but sorcery. Certainly, God is your Lord, who created the heaven and the earth in six days, and sits upon his Throne <note>original: "Zetel", referring to the Divine Throne or Arsh</note>, where he ordains all things; no one speaks for his neighbor <note>intercedes</note> without his permission. He is your God and Lord, worship him alone. Will you not reflect upon it? You shall all one day be gathered before him. He promises with truth that he shall cause men to die, and to rise again, in order to reward those who have believed in his Law and have performed good works. The unbelievers shall drink a seething <note>boiling</note> drink, and feel great pains for their wickedness. It is he who has given light to the sun, and brightness to the moon, and created the Signs <note>the phases of the moon or celestial markers</note>, to know the number of years, the reckoning of the months, and of all that which he has created. These things teach with truth the wonders of his divine Majesty to those who are able to know them. The distinction between day and night, and that which God has created in the heaven and on the earth, are signs of his unity to those who have his fear before their eyes. Those who believe there is no resurrection, those who place their contentment in the enjoyment of the goods of this world, those who trust in their riches, and those who are ignorant of God's commandments, shall be cast into the fires of hell for their sins; and the true believers [shall be led] by his divine Majesty into delightful gardens

# MAHOMET'S

### XVI. *Chapter of the Night Journey, containing one hundred and eleven verses, written at Mecca.*

Dear Reader, the Turks <note>A common 17th-century European term for Muslims in general</note> believe that Mahomet <note>Archaic spelling of Muhammad</note> climbed into the heavens during the night of this journey with the Angel Gabriel, and sat upon a white Buraq <note>original: "Burik"</note>, which is a beast; partly mule, partly donkey, and partly horse. He saw all the Prophets who had been before him, and all the wonders of Paradise. He spoke with God, who sat upon his throne. See the *Kitab al-Tanwir* <note>original: "Kitabel tenoir," a reference to a commentary or "Book of Illumination"</note>, the *Tafsir* <note>original: "Tesfyr," meaning Quranic commentary</note> of al-Jawzi, and the explanation of Jalaluddin <note>original: "Gélaldyn," likely referring to the Tafsir al-Jalalayn</note>. The *Bidaya* <note>original: "Bedati"</note> calls this the Chapter of the Children of Israel.

---

<margin>
Concerning the abandoning of their faith, and frequently taking it up again. See the *Kitab al-Tanwir*.
</margin>
IN the name of the kind and merciful God, Praise be to the one who by night caused his servant to go from the Temple of Mecca to the Temple of Jerusalem. We have blessed this Temple, and all that which is around it, as a sign of our omnipotence. We sent the Old Testament to Moses to instruct the children of Israel, and to forbid them from worshipping any other God but me, and also to forbid them from worshipping Noah’s lineage, nor the tribe of those whom we preserved in the Ark. ### *XIX. Chapter of Salvation and of Hell, containing one hundred and thirty-five lines, written at Mecca.*
<note>This refers to Sura 20, "Ta-Ha." The translator uses Roman numeral XIX, though in modern numbering it is Chapter 20.</note>

Dear Reader, the Mohammedans <note>A historical term for Muslims</note> have named this chapter *Tthe*. These are two letters of the Arabic alphabet, namely *Tt* and *He*. In this place, *Tt* signifies *Thouba*, which is Salvation, and *He* signifies *Haoihe*, which is Hell. See the explanation and commentary of Jalaluddin <note>original: "Gelaldyn," referring to the author of the Tafsir al-Jalalayn</note> and of al-Baydawi <note>original: "Bedaoi," a famous 13th-century Quranic scholar</note>. They have called this the chapter of Salvation and of Hell.

In the name of the kind and merciful God. We have not given the Quran to you to torment you, but to teach it to the pious. It is sent to you from Him who created the heaven and the earth. The Merciful One sits on His Throne: all that is in heaven, and on earth, and that which is between them, and under the earth, belongs to Him. He knows your thoughts. He knows that which you keep hidden, and that which you reveal.

### IN the name of the kind and merciful God. 

O man, I swear by the Quran, full of teaching, that you are a Prophet, sent to teach the people the right way. Remember our servant Job <note>The biblical Job, known in Arabic as Ayyub</note>, when he prayed to his Lord and said that the devil had overwhelmed him with misfortune and suffering. It was said to him: Strike the earth with your foot, you shall see water come out from it, to wash yourself and to drink. We have, through our special favor, restored to him his children and goods to serve as an example to posterity. When his wife wanted to make him grumble <note>or complain against God</note>, it was said to him: Take rods in your hand, strike your wife with them, and do not go against that which you have promised. We found him patient and zealous in obedience to our commandments. Remember our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, inclined and zealous toward our law: We have preserved them and chosen them among the good.

Those who keep my fear before their eyes shall enjoy the delights of the Garden of Eden, where they shall lean upon very beautiful beds: they shall have all kinds of fruits there, and delicious drinks; and their wives shall cast their eyes upon no one else but them. There you see that which has been promised to them on the Day of Judgment; and these delights shall never end.

The wicked and the unbelievers shall be thrust into the hellish fire, and drink seething water in abundance, and water that is cold beyond measure <note>referring to 'Zamhareer,' a place of extreme cold in hell</note>, and full of all kinds of stench. They shall be cast into the flame, and say to those who obeyed them on earth: May you be eternally tormented; you have misled us and made us wander. On the contrary, [the leaders say:] may you yourselves be tormented; you have been the cause of our misfortune, and shall be damned with us. They shall then say: Lord, increase the punishment of the one who is the cause of our disaster. Can we not see those whom we believed on earth to be unbelievers, and whom we mocked? ### XLVIII. *Chapter of the Enclosures, containing eighteen verses, written at Medina.* <note>This is Surah Al-Hujurat (The Chambers). While the text labels it 48, in modern numbering it is the 49th Surah.</note>

->Ekteri <note>likely referring to a specific commentator or translator</note> calls this the Chapter of the Walls.<-

IN the name of the kind and merciful God. O you who believe, do not place your own actions above that which is done by God and his Prophet, and fear God; he understands all that you say, and sees all that you do. O you who believe, when you speak to the Prophet, do not speak louder than he: do not shout as you do when you speak among one another; otherwise you shall make your good works vain and useless without knowing it. God has tested the virtue of those who speak softly in the presence of the Prophet: he has forgiven them their sins, and given a very great reward to them. Those who call to you from behind the enclosures <note>original: "heiningen"; referring to the private apartments of the Prophet's wives</note> do not know what they do: if they had waited until you had come out to them, they would have done very well. God is kind and merciful. O you who believe, if any unbeliever <note>original: "ongelovige"; often used here to mean a person of bad character or a liar</note> wishes to preach to you, then distinguish the truth from the lie: if you believe the ignorant, you shall have regret for it. Know that God's Apostle is among you. You shall anger God if you obey the unbelievers in many things. God wants you to embrace his law; it shall gladden your hearts, and cause you to have a horror of disobedience and wickedness: those who have a horror of such things are, through his special grace, firm in their faith; he knows them, and is very wise. ### XLIX. Chapter of the Decided Matter, containing
### forty-five lines, written at Mecca.

Mahomet <note>The Prophet Muhammad</note> named this Chapter after the letter *Kaf* of the Arabic alphabet, which in this place signifies *kda el emer* <note>original: "kda el emer"</note>, that is, the decided matter: see Galaldyn <note>Jalal al-Din al-Mahalli, a famous Quranic commentator</note> and Badaoi <note>Al-Baydawi, another prominent classical commentator</note>. They have called this the Chapter of the Sentence, or of the Decided Matter. Many Mahometans <note>Muslims</note> also say that *Kaf* is a mountain that surrounds this entire world, and that Mahomet swears by this mountain.

->IN the name of the kind and merciful God.<-

I swear by the Alkoran <note>The Quran</note>, which is praiseworthy, that the citizens of Mecha <note>Mecca</note> wonder that a man of their own nation teaches them of the pains of hell. They say that he speaks strange things. "How!" they say; "shall we die? shall we become earth and return again to the world? See, that is a strange return." We know certainly what the earth shall do with them. We have a book <term>Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz)</term> in which everything is written. They fight against the known truth and are in great confusion. Do they not see the heaven above them, and that we have built and adorned it? and how it has no defect? We have stretched out the earth, raised the mountains, and brought forth all kinds of fruits as proof of our omnipotence. We have sent the blessed rain from heaven, caused gardens to sprout there, produced seed that is pleasing to the mower <note>original: "majer," meaning reaper or harvester</note>, and caused palm trees, one higher than the other, to grow up to enrich our creatures; we have thereby given life to the dead, dry, and barren earth: thus shall the dead also come forth from their graves.

### LV. *Chapter of the Judgment, containing ninety-nine verses, written at Medina.*

IN the name of the kind and merciful God, the day of Judgment shall come: no one can deny it. On this day many shall be tested and humbled, and many shall be exalted and joyful. <margin>The blessed.
The damned.
The Prophets.</margin>

From the first ages there shall be many, and from the last ages few. They shall rest on beds adorned with gold and precious stones, and all look one another in the face. Young children shall go around them with vessels, bowls, and cups full of a pleasant drink <note>original: "aangename drank," likely referring to non-intoxicating wine</note>, which shall not give them a headache, nor make them drunk. They shall have all the fruits they can wish for, and such food as they shall desire. They shall have women with black eyes, and as white as strings of pearls, as a reward for their good works. They shall hear no evil words spoken, nor sin, and shall constantly hear the voices of those who bless them.

### LXII. *Chapter of the Wicked, containing eleven verses, written at Medina.* <note>This is Surah 63, commonly known as "Al-Munafiqun" or The Hypocrites. The translator uses "Bozen" (Wicked/Evil ones) to describe them.</note>

IN the name of the kind and merciful God. When the wicked come to visit you, they shall say that they bear witness that you are a Prophet sent by God; He knows well that you are His Prophet: He sees that they feign <note>original: "veinzen" - to pretend or act hypocritically</note>, and sell their faith to possess goods in the world; in which they do evil. They say with the mouth, "We believe in God's law," and are wicked in their souls. Wickedness is pressed into their hearts, and they shall not understand the mysteries of the faith. The beauty of their bodies shall not displease you when you see them. They stand tall when they speak, and seem like a piece of wood leaning against a wall. <note>A metaphor for their lack of internal substance or spiritual life despite their outward appearance.</note> They fear all running rumors and are your enemies. Guard yourself against them; God shall without doubt destroy them. How can they blaspheme His law? When it was said to them: "Come to the Prophet, he shall request forgiveness from God for your sins"; they shook their heads and departed with arrogance. Calamity is upon them: whether you request forgiveness for them or not, God shall not forgive them; He does not love the wicked. ### *LXIX. Chapter of the Ascent, containing forty-four lines, written at Mecca.*

IN the name of the kind and merciful God. Some people have asked when the Day of Judgment shall be, and at what time the wicked shall be punished. No one other than God can deliver men from the pains of hell. He is master of the way that climbs to heaven. The Angels and the Spirits shall ascend to him on the Day of Judgment. This day shall seem to the wicked to last fifty thousand years. Wait with patience. The wicked believe that they are still far from this day; but you shall see it soon. On this day the heaven shall appear like molten metal. The mountains shall be like carded wool that falls down, and no one shall ask his neighbor what it is. They shall look upon one another. The wicked shall wish to buy themselves free from these pains with the loss of their children, wives, brothers, companions, neighbors, and with the loss of all that is upon the earth. ### LXXVII. *Chapter of the Tidings, containing forty lines, written at Mecca.* <note>This is Surah An-Naba (The Tidings), usually numbered as the 78th Surah in modern editions.</note>

IN the name of the kind and merciful God. What do the wicked ask of one another regarding the great tidings, about which they differ in opinion? They shall understand it; they shall understand it. Have I not created and stretched out the earth? Have I not raised the mountains to fasten them? Have we not created you male and female? Have we not created sleep and the night for resting, and the day for laboring? Have we not built seven heavens and the sun full of light above you? Have we not made the water come down from the clouds, to make the earth bring forth its plants and many kinds of herbs? The Day of Judgment shall one day be a day of joy and sorrow. When the Angel shall blow the trumpet, shall all the world come in a throng to the General Judgment? The heaven shall open its door, the mountains shall move; and hell is the place prepared for the strayed. They shall remain there eternally. They shall find no rest there, nor any drink, but boiling and stinking water; a retribution that well corresponds with their works. ### LXXXIV. Chapter of the Heavenly Signs, containing twenty lines, written at Mecca.

IN the name of the kind and merciful God. He created his throne, to which one owes eternal praise. Certainly, the Alkoran, which is precious, stands written in the book which is preserved in heaven.

## To the
# R E A D E R .

Worthy Reader, since we have presented to you the Alkoran <note>The Quran; the central religious text of Islam</note>, or the Lawbook of the Mohammedans <note>A historical term for Muslims, common in the 17th century</note>, as they define it, it shall in our judgment not be improper that we also speak somewhat of him who is called the Maker, or otherwise the Receiver thereof (since they claim that this book has come down from heaven). And since friends and enemies have written of his descent, birth, upbringing, and deeds, each (as is to be believed) according to the various passions by which he was driven, we shall here present a twofold account of his life and conduct. First, a description of his life and deeds from the Saracen History of Georgius Elmacinus <note>original: "Georgius Elmacinus"; Al-Makin ibn al-Amid (1205–1273), a Coptic Christian historian who wrote in Arabic; the translator here mistakenly identifies him as a "Mohammedan"</note>, who, being a follower of Mohammed, wrote in the Arabic language. The other description is drawn from the writings of various Christian Authors, his opponents, and indeed mostly in their own words, but not set down in the same order; since we, to avoid all confusion as much as possible, have taken from each Author that which we judged useful for the purpose, following the sequence of time from his birth until his death, and [joining them] together—

<summary>This preface introduces a biography of the Prophet Muhammad, explaining that the work will provide two perspectives: one from an Arabic historical source and another compiled from various Christian accounts.</summary>
<keywords>Quran, Muhammad, Georgius Elmacinus, Saracen History, biography, religious polemics, 17th-century translation</keywords>

--- Page 498 ---
<meta>Continuity from previous page: The author is concluding the introductory remarks regarding the methodology of compiling various accounts of Islamic history and theology. Catchword: M A (likely referring to Mahomet).</meta>

have set down, without attempting to reconcile the points in which they differ, both to avoid entangling ourselves in an incorrect judgment in such obscure matters, and also so that the attentive reader might notice the differences and contradictions therein for himself, and if he so pleases, judge them according to his own preference. We add here also a presentation, fabricated by Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"; the text uses the older European spelling for the Prophet of Islam</note> and his followers, of a journey to Jerusalem, and further to heaven, with the incredible <term>spoorelose dingen</term> <note>literally "trackless things," meaning extraordinary or irrational events that leave no logical trace</note> which he, as it is told, saw there. Added to this is a Dialogue <note>original: "Samenspraak"</note> between a Jew and Muhammad, who gives him an account and explanation of his teaching. This is what we had to say here. Proceed now as you please, and fare well.

*Drawn from the Saracen History of George Elmacin <note>original: "Georgius Elmacinus," a 13th-century Christian Arab historian</note>, written in the Arabic language, and set into Latin by Thomas Erpenius <note>A famous Dutch Orientalist and professor at Leiden University</note>, and translated from that by J.H.G.*

<margin>Muhammad’s descent.</margin>
Muhammad Abulkasim, son of Abdalla, who was a son of Abdulmutalib, who was a son of Hashim, and who in turn was a son of Abdumenaf, was the first who brought the religion of Islamism <note>The term "Islamismum" here refers to the faith of Islam</note> into the light and maintained it. The name of his mother was Amina, who was a daughter of Wahb, the son of Abdumenaf.

<margin>Fatherland, birth.</margin>
Muhammad, of glorious memory, was born in the urban valley of the City of Mecca, on Monday at the break of day, which was the eighth of the month of the first Rabi <note>Rabi' al-awwal, the third month of the Islamic calendar</note>, which corresponds with the twenty-second day of the month of Nisan <note>April</note> from the months of the Romans, in the eight hundred and eighty-second year of Alexander the Great <note>This refers to the Seleucid era, often used in Middle Eastern chronologies of this period</note>.

<margin>Upbringing.</margin>
His father died two months before he was born, and his mother when he was six years old. He was therefore raised by his grandfather Abdulmutalib until he had reached eight years; for then he also died, at the age of one hundred and ten years: and from then on he was excellently raised by his father's brother, named Abu Talib.

<margin>Calling.</margin>
When he had reached forty years, he was called (to the Prophetic office) on Monday, which was the second day of the month of the first Rabi, in the nine hundred and twenty-second year of

He entered Mecca without engaging in battle; and all the people of this city believed, except for a few, whom he put to death with the shedding of their blood. Mecca was won on the twenty-first day of the month of Ramadan <note>original: "Radaman"; the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, observed as a month of fasting</note>, and this occurred in peace and quiet before any force was used.

<margin>Battle.</margin>
In this year also occurred the battle of Hunayn <note>original: "Honaina"</note>, a very well-known valley. For when the Hawazin <note>original: "Hawasins"</note> understood that Mecca had been won, they gathered together under Malik, son of Awf <note>original: "Melik, Aufs zoon"</note>, where the Thaqif <note>original: "Tsekifs"</note>, with their wives and treasures, also joined them. Muhammad marched against them with twelve thousand men. These two armies fell upon each other in the valley of Hunayn. The infidels gained the first victory: but afterwards the Muslims regained the upper hand, putting them to flight and plundering all their treasures. This booty consisted of six thousand oxen, twenty-four thousand goats, forty thousand sheep, and four thousand ounces of silver. In this battle, ninety men of the Thaqif were killed, and no more than four men of the Muslims were slain. All the captured women and the booty of al-Ji'ranah <note>original: "Gjarana"</note> were gathered together, and he marched away against Ta'if <note>original: "Tajifa"</note>, which he besieged. But later, abandoning this siege, he went to al-Ji'ranah, where the captured women of the Hawazin were; their ambassadors came to him and requested that he would graciously return their wives to them, saying moreover that they were his paternal aunts <note>A reference to Muhammad's nursing among the Banu Sa'd, a subgroup of the Hawazin</note>. He therefore gave them the choice between their wives and children, or their treasures. They chose their wives and children, whom he returned to them; and he distributed their treasures among the Muslims.

In the same year, Malik, son of Awf, came to him at al-Ji'ranah and believed. He therefore restored his property to him and made Attab, son of Asid <note>original: "Gajat, Aseds zoon"</note>, governor of Mecca.

# LIFE.

<margin>Age and nature.</margin>
He was fifty-five years old. He was of a clever wit: pleasant of voice, and visited and received his kin, just as they visited and received him. He cared for the poor, praised the great, socialized with the small, and let no one who requested something of him go without that which he requested, or at least without kind words from him.

<margin>Scribes.</margin>
His Scribes <note>The secretaries responsible for recording revelations and state correspondence</note> were Uthman, son of Affan, and Ali, son of Abu Talib. Sometimes Ubayy, son of Ka'b, and Zayd, son of Thabit, also wrote for him. He occasionally used other Scribes whom he had with him, namely Muawiyah, son of Abu Sufyan, Khalid, son of Sa'id (who was the son of Abulas), Al-Ala, son of al-Hadrami, and Hanzala, son of Rabi. Abdallah, son of Abi Sarh, who defected from Islam <note>original: "Iſlamiſmum"</note> and joined the infidels, also wrote for him: However, Uthman requested a pardon for him during the time of victory, which Muhammad granted him after he had previously decided to shed his blood. Zubayr, son of al-Awwam, and Jahm, son of Safwan, recorded the alms; Hudhayfah, son of al-Yaman <note>The text reads Hadakias Semals zoon, likely a transcription variant of Hudhayfah</note>, kept the account of the income from dates; and Mughira, son of Shu'ba, and Husayn, son of Jaman, wrote down the judgments and commands. But Abdallah, son of Arqam, answered the letters of the Princes.

<margin>His judges.</margin>
As for the judges who were in his time, he appointed over the oath Ali, son of Abu Talib, Mu'adh of Medina, son of Jabal, and Abu Musa of Ash'ari. The chief of his pardons was Anas, son of Malik, and Qays of Medina, son of Sa'id, was the chief of the bodyguard. <margin>banner</margin> His great banner was white, and his small banner black. <margin>Motto.</margin> In his seal was written: FOR A DOUBLE TESTIMONY <note>Likely referring to the Shahada, the dual testimony of faith</note>. <margin>The Era of the Hegira.</margin>
The Historian says: Since the Era of the Hegira <term>Hegira: the migration of Muhammad from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, marking the start of the Islamic calendar</term> marks the lunar years, we shall relate and instruct how many solar years are derived therefrom, in order to have a correct Chronology from the time of Adam, of pious memory, down to this present time. It is related, therefore, that Muhammad died after the passing of six thousand one hundred and twenty-three solar years, nine months, and fourteen days; at which time ten lunar years and seventy days of the Hegira Era had passed, which is nine solar years and eleven months minus one day. For the first day of the Hegira was a Thursday, and the last of his life a Monday; which together make three thousand six hundred and fourteen days.

<margin>Muhammad's inclination toward the Christians.</margin>
The Chronicles of the Christians report that he was well-disposed toward the Christians, and was friendly and gentle toward them: and that, when some of them came to him and sought safety from him, he merely imposed a tribute <note>likely referring to the Jizya tax</note> upon them, treated them well, and received them upon his word, saying to Omar: "Tell them that we esteem their souls as highly as we hold our own souls, and place their riches in the same state as ours, and their fortunes equal with ours." This is related by the author of the book *Al-Muhadhdhab* <note>original: "Almuhaddeb"; a significant work of Islamic jurisprudence</note>, from which the renowned Abu Hanifa <note>founder of the Hanafi school of Islamic law</note> brings this forward in the passage where he deals with a Muslim killing a Christian. Anyone who examines the descriptions of ancient histories concerning Mahomet will find (as commonly happens in things that grow from small to great, whose beginnings are usually obscure) such great differences therein, that he will hardly discover the truth of this history (if it is still to be found there). This light passed from Seth to Enos, and from him to his son Cainan <note>original: "Chanan"; likely referring to the biblical Kenan</note>, and thus subsequently from hand to hand down to Abraham, in whom it was doubled; one part thereof came to Ishmael, and from him to Kedar, from whom Muhammad was descended; and the other part passed to Isaac, who is the lineage of Christ’s generation. These things, brought forward by Muhammad and his followers, although they seem to be said by chance and unexpectedly, are nevertheless for the most part drawn from the Talmudists and Kabbalists <note>The author suggests that Islamic tradition borrows heavily from Jewish rabbinical and mystical commentaries</note>.

But to return again to Muhammad: they say that Ishmael, Abraham’s illegitimate son, from whom Muhammad reckoned his descent, came to live in Mecca, where he married Alghadira, the daughter of Alierchamin, King of that region, and by her had twelve children, who were all, like him, idolaters, and spread themselves from there into various regions: but the second, named Kedar, remained in Mecca, where his father had already built the previously mentioned tower and temple, which is called by Muhammad, in his Quran <note>original: "Alkoran"</note>, the first of all others, and of which he also says that it was established by Abraham himself. Kedar placed the idol in the tower, where it was thereafter always worshipped, until Muhammad, having found the means to establish his teaching and to win Mecca, destroyed this image: but the tower remained in its entirety; and the pilgrims go there to fulfill their vows. Kedar also had a black stone placed there, namely on the outside, toward the place where this idol was, so that those who went into the temple would know which way they had to turn. This stone, called "the fortunate" from all times, is still today greatly honored by the Muslims <note>original: "mahometanen"</note>, who bow before it and kiss it with great humility.

# MAHOMET

<margin>His Parents.</margin> tivia in Spain, since converted to the Christian faith, places it in the six hundred and twentieth year of our salvation; but there is no one who places his birth so late. Joannes Leo of Africa <note>Leo Africanus, a famous 16th-century traveler and geographer</note>, speaking of the year of the Hegira <term>Hegira: the migration of Muhammad from Mecca to Medina, marking the start of the Islamic calendar</term>, or flight; (which was the fifty-second or fifty-third year of Mahomet's life) places that in the five hundred and ninety-first year of our salvation, although it occurred in the ninety-third year <note>likely referring to 593 AD</note>. Palmerius, and after him Funk, Nikolaas Zeno, and many others place this era-year of the Hegira in the six hundredth year after Christ's birth. Vulgand Dresser, in his Saracen Chronology, brings his birth to the five hundred and sixty-seventh year, and the completion of his Alkoran <note>The Quran</note> to the six hundred and twenty-third year; in such a way that fifty-seven years passed between them—although he places his death in the fortieth year of his age. Celius Augustinus Kurio places his birth in the five hundred and sixty-third year, and his death in the six hundred and thirty-seventh year, after he had ruled for ten years. The time of his reign is indeed true; but according to his calculation, he would have lived seventy-seven years, which is wrong: and he, not having made his calculation well, says that the fifteen hundred and sixty-seventh year—when he prepared his Alkoran—was the nine hundredth year since the establishment of the Saracen Empire: in such a way that it had only begun in the six hundred and sixty-seventh year, thirty years after the death of this deceiver; even though all the Mahometans <note>archaic term for Muslims</note> unanimously count their years of the Hegira from that time in which Mahomet, with his followers, was forced to flee from Mecca, ten years before he passed away.

Mahomet, as far as that is concerned, was a son of one of the most prominent citizens of Mecca named Abdalla <note>Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib</note>, son of Abdalmutalif, of the tribe of Korais <note>The Quraysh tribe</note>, and of a mother named Emyna <note>Aminah bint Wahb</note>, who, as it is claimed, was a Jewess, and young...

He was born in the city of Jetrib or Jefrab <note>Modern Medina; the text reflects older European transliterations</note>, which for this reason has since been called *Medina Albani* <note>original: "Medina Albani"; likely a corruption of Madinat al-Nabi</note>, the city of the Prophet, twelve or fifteen miles on this side of Mecca—or, according to others, in Mecca itself, which is a very famous harbor in the western part of Arabia Felix <note>original: "gelukkig Arabien"; the fertile southern/western region of the Arabian peninsula</note>, thirty or forty miles from the Red Sea, where all the fragrant herbs and spices, and other precious wares from the region of the Sabaeans <note>An ancient South Arabian civilization, famous for the biblical Queen of Sheba</note> arrive by caravans on camels. When Mahomet was born, this city was inhabited partly by Jews, who had their own Temples and Schools, and partly by Heathens, who worshipped a goddess named Alieche Aluza <note>Al-Uzza, one of the three chief goddesses of Arabian Neopaganism</note>, whom people considered to be the goddess Venus. And from this it may have come that the Mahometans celebrate Friday (just as the Jews do Saturday, and the Christians Sunday) in memory of this goddess, who formerly among the Heathens represented the goddess of generation and fertility; for Mahomet secretly retained many things from the old Heathenism at Mecca. There were also many Christians mingled among them; such as Nestorians, Jacobites <note>Two distinct Eastern Christian denominations often cited in early Islamic history</note>, and others of a similar sort. There was also a Temple in the middle of the city called *Beithalla* <note>Bayt Allah</note>, that is, God's house, with a tower called *Elkabba* or *Alkibel* <note>The Kaaba or the Qibla (direction of prayer)</note>, toward which the Mahometans commonly turned when they performed their *Zalla* <note>Salat</note>, or prayer; (today they all turn toward the south) and swore by its name, as the Moors still do today; such great reverence do they show to it.

In this book, it is also recounted that when he had reached the age of four or five years and was playing with his fellow boys, three men unexpectedly arrived, who took him from the midst of them all and led him to the top of a mountain not far from there. There, one of them opened his chest and belly down to the navel with a pair of shears and washed his entrails with snow; the second cut his heart into two parts and took from the middle of it a small black grain, which he threw away, saying, "This is the devil's portion"; and the third cleansed the wound and healed it again as it was before. 

<margin>He outweighs ten men.</margin> Having done this, they placed him in one of the pans of a large scale, and in the other pan ten strong and heavy-bodied men, whom he outweighed; whereupon they said: "Let us depart from this child, for a great number of men would not be able to outweigh him." And they, having kissed him on the head and the forehead, departed from there and vanished.

Then the same voice came again, saying to him: "Let them be, for the Savior of Israel is already born." Elijah, asking where he was, received as an answer from the voice: "In Bethlehem of Judah." He went there and found a woman sitting on the threshold of her door, with a child, a son, stretched out before her and covered in blood. He said to the woman: "My daughter, have you borne a son?" "Yes," she said. "And what," he asked again, "does it mean that he is thus bloodied?" She answered: "A great evil has occurred; on the same day that he was born, the House of the Sanctuary was destroyed." "My daughter," he answered her, "do not be dismayed; only be diligent in raising him, for from him a very great salvation shall come forth for the whole world." She, being suddenly enlightened and strengthened by this, devoted herself to nourishing him diligently; and thereupon Elijah departed from her. Five years later he remembered this again and said to himself: "I shall return, in order to..."

While Elijah was still speaking with her, the winds from all four corners of the earth came blowing upon the child and carried him away to a great sea. Elijah thereupon began to tear his clothes, and to pull out his hair and beard with great crying, shouting: "Alas! The salvation of Israel is lost!" But the daughter of the voice <note>original: "dochter van de stem" (Hebrew: *Bat Kol*), referring to a divine echo or heavenly proclamation.</note>, that is, the revelation, came thereupon, saying to him: "O Elijah, the matter goes not as you say; for he shall be for four hundred years in the great sea, and eighty years in the rising of the smoke among the children of Korah, and also as long at the gate of Rome; and for the remainder of the years he shall return through all the great cities, until the end of the appointed time."

All of this is contained word for word in the recounted passage, and we have placed it here to show what kinship the fables of the Mohammedans <note>A historical term for Muslims, used here in a comparative religious context.</note> have with the stories of the Talmudists and Rabbis.
